lesson.title: Beyond Correlation: What It Takes to Claim Causation
lesson.summary: Causation means that changing one variable directly produces a change in another, a claim that generally requires a well-designed randomized experiment rather than an observed association alone.
lesson.body:
An association between two variables tells you they tend to move together, but it does not, by itself, tell you why. Causation is the much stronger claim that a change in one variable directly produces a change in another. Establishing causation is harder than establishing association, because association can arise from causation, but it can also arise from a lurking variable, from chance, or from the two variables being different measurements of nearly the same underlying thing.

The most reliable way to establish causation is a well-designed, randomly assigned experiment. Random assignment is the key ingredient: when subjects are placed into treatment and control groups purely by chance, any lurking variables (age, health, motivation, soil quality, whatever might otherwise confound the result) get spread out roughly evenly between the groups on average. That balancing act means that if the groups end up with substantially different outcomes, the treatment itself is the most plausible explanation, since nothing else was allowed to differ systematically between the groups.

Here is a simple illustration. Suppose an agricultural researcher wants to know whether a new fertilizer increases crop yield. Twenty otherwise similar plots of land are randomly assigned, ten to receive the new fertilizer and ten to receive none, with every other growing condition (water, sunlight, soil type) held as similar as possible across both groups. At harvest, the fertilized plots average 145 bushels per acre and the unfertilized plots average 130 bushels per acre, a 15 bushel difference. Because the plots were randomly assigned to groups, that 15 bushel gap cannot be easily blamed on some other systematic difference between the groups (both groups should have similar amounts of good and bad soil, sunny and shaded spots, on average), which makes the fertilizer a credible cause of the higher yield.

Contrast that with simply observing which farmers already happen to use this fertilizer and comparing their yields to farmers who do not. Farmers who choose to buy and apply fertilizer might also tend to have better equipment, more fertile land to begin with, or more farming experience, any of which could be a lurking variable producing a yield difference even if the fertilizer itself did nothing. Without random assignment, there is no guarantee those other factors are balanced between the groups, so an observed yield difference could reflect the fertilizer, the lurking variables, or some mixture of both.

This is why AP Statistics draws such a sharp line between experiments and other kinds of studies: only the random assignment of an experiment gives you real grounds for a causal claim. Every other kind of study can reveal association, sometimes a strong and reproducible one, but claiming causation from it requires ruling out lurking variables by some other means, which is far harder to do convincingly.
